issues.html:
Hello again, and welcome to issue #3! 👋

This week the world's biggest code platform rebuilt itself around AI agents, two new models landed, and AI chip money got even bigger. Five minutes, tops. Let's go.

📡 The Big Signal: GitHub rebuilds itself around AI agents

In short: GitHub launched a new Copilot app where AI agents do the work across your projects and you approve the results.

At GitHub Universe on Wednesday (28 October), GitHub said its goal is now "completed software work", not more code. The centrepiece is the GitHub Copilot app: you give it a goal and some context, it runs as many agents as the job needs across several repositories, and it brings back pull requests for you to review.

Alongside it came Copilot Fusion, which picks the right model (or mix of models) for each task, a deeper "Max" level of Copilot code review, and sessions you can start on your phone and pick up in VS Code. The commercial twist: GitHub Enterprise customers now get every Copilot feature without a separate subscription, paying for the AI credits they use.

Why this matters: writing code is becoming the cheap part; the skill that counts is deciding what to build and checking what the agents hand back.

Sources: GitHub blog · GitHub Changelog

⚡ Quick Hits

In short: OpenAI released a fast, cheaper model that's good at using a computer for you.

OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra halves the price. Terra is built for everyday work such as understanding images, filling in forms and coding, and its API price is 50% lower than GPT-5.6 Terra's, at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output. OpenAI says it more than doubles its predecessor's score on the Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding test and makes far fewer factual errors. OpenAI

Why this matters: jobs like typing invoice details into accounting software are getting cheap enough to hand to AI at scale.

In short: Google's newest top model is built to find and fix security holes.

Google's Gemini 4 Carbon puts security first. Just two weeks after Argon, Google announced Carbon, which tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and scores 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for finding real software vulnerabilities. It's going to a small group of cyber defenders first, with wider access promised "as soon as possible" at $2/$10 per million tokens. Google

Why this matters: AI that can find security holes this well is useful to attackers too, which is why Google is giving it to defenders first.

In short: banks are lending $63 billion so Anthropic can rent Broadcom's AI chips.

A $63B loan to rent AI chips. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley are funding a new company that will buy Broadcom's AI accelerators and networking gear and lease them to Anthropic, with deliveries from 2027. Broadcom is backing part of the financing itself. Broadcom

Why this matters: AI chips are now financed like aircraft or buildings, which shows how much capital the AI build-out is soaking up.

In short: Europe is getting the world's first large-scale factory for a more efficient kind of power chip.

Infineon bets €1.1B on gallium nitride in Austria. Infineon will turn existing cleanrooms in Villach into the world's first high-volume plant for gallium nitride (GaN) power chips on 300mm wafers, with production due by the end of 2027. Bigger wafers yield 2.3 times as many chips each, and the EU has approved €319 million in state aid. Infineon

Why this matters: GaN chips waste less electricity as heat, and AI data centres badly need to save power.

🛠️ Tool of the Week: Local Code

In short: a free, open-source AI assistant for the Mac that runs entirely on your own computer.

Draw Things has released Local Code, an AI agent that writes and reviews code, edits spreadsheets and slides, makes images and can work with your Mac's Mail, Notes and Calendar, all without sign-ins, API keys or sending your files to the cloud. Smaller models run on Macs with 16GB of memory; the biggest wants 64GB or more. The whole app is open source (GPL-3.0) on GitHub.

Why this matters: if privacy rules stop you pasting work files into ChatGPT, a capable assistant that never leaves your machine is a real alternative.

👉 Read the launch post

💡 One Takeaway

Get good at reviewing, not just prompting. GitHub, OpenAI and Google all pitched the same future this week: agents do the work, and you check it. Start practising now. When AI hands you code, a draft or a spreadsheet, read it as if a new colleague wrote it: test the claims, run the code, and ask what's missing. That habit will matter more than any single tool.

That's issue #3! What did you make of it? Just hit reply: we read every message, and we'd love to know what you want more (or less) of.

And if Signal Tech saved you some scrolling this week, forward it to a friend who'd enjoy it. That's how we grow.

Until next Friday, The Signal Tech team 📡 The tech that matters, minus the noise.

issues.html:
Hello again, and welcome to issue #2! 👋

This week AI stopped just writing code and started finding the holes in it, at internet scale. Plus a new kind of assistant, a big bet on open chips and a very cheap model. Five minutes, tops. Let's go.

📡 The Big Signal: AI finds critical PHP flaws, and everyone needs to patch

In short: two serious security holes in PHP, the language behind a huge share of websites, are now fixed. Update now.

On Wednesday (21 October), PHP shipped versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 to fix two critical bugs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that can let an attacker run their own code on a server without logging in. PHP's maintainers say every installation serving web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php and FrankenPHP, and that updating is the only complete fix. PHP 8.1 and older get no official update, so ask your vendor or upgrade.

The twist: security firm Calif found one of the flaws using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, as part of OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" programme, and Wiz found both independently. CISA, the US cyber agency, says it hasn't seen attacks yet, but urges organisations to patch immediately, starting with internet-facing systems.

Why this matters: if your website, shop or blog runs on PHP (WordPress does), ask whoever hosts it to confirm it's updated this week.

Sources: PHP security advisory · CISA · OpenAI

⚡ Quick Hits

In short: Anthropic launched an assistant that messages you first.

Claude Duet wants to be your proactive co-worker. Anthropic opened a waitlist research preview of Claude Duet, an app built around Claude Opus 5.5 that sends a morning brief, keeps an eye on your connected apps and works in the background on its own virtual machine. It asks your approval before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs anything or deletes something, and starts with US Pro and Max subscribers. Anthropic

Why this matters: AI assistants are shifting from "wait to be asked" to "tap you on the shoulder", so how much you let them see is becoming a real choice.

In short: OpenAI's models are coming to Google's cloud.

OpenAI lands on Google Cloud. OpenAI's frontier models and Codex agent workflows are heading to Google Cloud's Model Garden, with general availability planned in the coming weeks. Businesses will be able to pay for them from existing Google Cloud commitments, though OpenAI says Microsoft remains its primary cloud partner. OpenAI

Why this matters: if your company already runs on Google Cloud, using OpenAI's models may soon need no new contract.

In short: a RISC-V chip start-up raised $1.5 billion.

Tenstorrent more than doubles its value. Jim Keller's Tenstorrent closed a $1.5B Series E at a $6.2B valuation, led by Trace Capital and Innovation X. It will spend the money deploying its Galaxy servers at scale and growing the RISC-V CPU and AI chip designs it licenses to firms such as Samsung and LG. Tenstorrent

Why this matters: investors are paying serious money for alternatives to NVIDIA, which could mean more choice and cheaper AI hardware over time.

In short: a strong AI model that costs pennies to run.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash goes cheap. MiniMax released M3.1 Flash, a model aimed at agents, coding and computer use, priced at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output. The company says it is nearly three times faster than its predecessor and cuts the cost of agent tasks by 70%. MiniMax

Why this matters: when capable models cost this little, it becomes affordable to let AI handle long, many-step jobs.

🛠️ Tool of the Week: VegaLoad

In short: a free, open-source tool that checks your app copes with heavy traffic.

The founders of LitmusChaos have launched VegaLoad, an Apache 2.0 load tester that ships as one small binary for macOS, Linux, Windows, Docker and Kubernetes. It speaks 14 protocols (HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis and more), has a built-in MCP server so Cursor or Claude Code can write and run tests for you, and can fail a pull request when latency or error limits are broken. Hosts other than localhost need your approval, and every run writes a single offline HTML report.

Why this matters: finding out your app falls over under load is far cheaper before launch day than during it.

👉 Read the launch post

💡 One Takeaway

Know what versions you're running. This week's PHP scramble was hardest for teams who didn't know where PHP lived in their stack. Keep a simple list of every language, framework and runtime version behind your projects, and subscribe to their security announcement lists. When the next "update now" lands, you'll know in minutes whether it's your problem.

issues.html:
Hello, and welcome to the very first Signal Tech! 👋

You're one of our founding readers, and we're chuffed to have you. Here's the deal: every week we pick out the tech stories that actually matter in AI, chips and dev tools, explain them in plain English, and skip the hype. Five minutes, tops. Let's get into it.

📡 The Big Signal: Google finally ships Gemini 4 Argon

On Tuesday (13 October), Google released Gemini 4 Argon, its new flagship AI model. It's available now to developers and businesses through the Gemini API and AI Studio, and to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search. Google says Argon is built for "deep work": long, complex jobs in coding, science, cybersecurity and agent-style tasks, with a 1-million-token limit via the API.

Why it matters: this is Google's first major frontier release since Gemini 3 in late 2025, after months of watching OpenAI and Anthropic pull ahead. Reuters notes Google had already scrapped plans for Gemini 3.5 Pro. Pricing is the bit to watch if you build with it: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens at launch, rising to $4 and $20 after 30 November. Try it now while it's cheap, and do your sums before you commit.

Sources: Google · The Verge · Reuters via Yahoo

⚡ Quick Hits

AI chip designers can write the code, not finish the job. ChipAgents and NVIDIA launched Build-A-Chip-Bench, which tests whether AI agents can take a chip from spec all the way to a finished physical layout. Tested agents passed functional checks on about 40% of tasks, but only around 10% hit their performance, power and area targets. ChipAgents

NVIDIA wants AI running the fab, too. At SEMICON West on 14 October, NVIDIA announced cuPotential, an early-access library for simulating how atoms and molecules interact, which it says sped up already GPU-optimised workflows by a further 2-3x in testing. It also said the open-source NanoVDB library helped Lam Research run chipmaking simulations 30x faster. NVIDIA

A 24B model built to run on your laptop. Liquid AI released LFM2.5-24B-A2B, an open-weight model designed for on-device agents, with a 131,072-token context window and downloads on Hugging Face. Its demo showed the model calling tools on a MacBook Pro without any cloud API calls. AI.info

Meta's crowded week. Argon landed just a day after Meta announced its own frontier model, Muse Wonder Full. The takeaway: the AI race is very much not a two-horse affair any more. The Verge

🛠️ Tool of the Week: ML Drift

Google has open-sourced ML Drift (Apache 2.0), the GPU engine behind its LiteRT on-device AI runtime. It hides the messy differences between OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal and WebGPU, so one model can run fast on Android, iOS, the web and desktop. If you still use the old TFLite GPU delegate, note that it won't get new features any more. Google says ML Drift is fully backwards compatible, so switching should be painless.
👉 Read the announcement

💡 One Takeaway

Watch the "introductory" price tags. Argon's API price doubles after 30 November. Before you build anything on a new model, put a rough cost estimate in your README (tokens per request × requests per day × price), then work it out again at the full price. If the numbers only add up during the discount, you want to know now, not at invoice time.
